settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The keepRegion mechanism (lines 334-336 and 817-826) keeps only boundary.length bytes across refills, which bounds repeated re-scanning of the same data and addresses a different, earlier DoS class; it does not, however, bound boundary.length itself.

Headers of each part are capped at HEADER_PART_SIZE_MAX = 10240 bytes (lines 176-179, enforced at lines 538-542), but this limit applies to part headers, not to the Content-Type request header carrying the boundary.
The buffer is fixed at DEFAULT_BUFSIZE = 4096 (line 184) unless a custom size is supplied, so makeAvailable() reads bounded chunks; only the per-byte comparison work scales with boundary length.

Direct MultipartStream(InputStream, byte[], int) usage (lines 301-303) lets an application choose bufSize, and many containers impose their own request/header size limits that would cap the boundary in practice.
candidates.description: MultipartStream's central constructor computes the delimiter array directly from the caller-supplied boundary byte array without any maximum-length check. It evaluates boundary.length in the array sizing (specifically new byte[boundary.length + BOUNDARY_PREFIX.length], the derived boundaryLength, and keepRegion = boundary.length), then copies the caller bytes. The same boundaryLength drives the inner comparison loop in findSeparator(), which is invoked from ItemInputStream construction (constructor at line 811 calls findSeparator()) and after every buffer refill in makeAvailable() (line 1010). When the buffer contains bytes that repeatedly match only the initial byte of the boundary (for example many CR bytes, since boundary[0] is CR after BOUNDARY_PREFIX), findByte returns positions that each trigger up to boundaryLength byte comparisons inside the for(match = 1; match < boundaryLength; match++) loop. A large boundary therefore multiplies the work done per buffered byte, and the full boundary string is materialized in a heap array whose size is derived from the attacker-controlled header value. This is the structural precondition underlying the historical boundary-length DoS class. Reachability/severity depend entirely on how FileUploadBase.getBoundary() (which parses the Content-Type header) and parseRequest() validate the boundary before constructing MultipartStream; those methods lie outside the source lines that were actually read, so exploitation is not established here.
missing_evidence: FileUploadBase.getBoundary() and parseRequest() (not among the read spans) were not inspected; a boundary length check there would neutralize this candidate.
No evidence of any FileUploadBase sizeMax/fileSizeMax enforcement path was read beyond their fields (lines 161-167, defaults -1).
No runtime measurement or proof that findSeparator's match loop produces disproportionate CPU on a large boundary was performed; the complexity argument is qualitative.
Container-level request header limits (e.g. servlet container max header size) that would bound boundary length were not examined.
preconditions: Application parses untrusted multipart requests with FileUploadBase.parseRequest (or directly uses MultipartStream with a boundary taken from the request Content-Type header).
The Content-Type/boundary value is not length-checked by the caller before MultipartStream construction, and the container does not independently cap the request header size.

Request body is attacker-controlled and can be shaped to contain many bytes equal to the first delimiter byte (e.g. CR) to maximize failed match attempts, or, for the memory angle, the boundary string itself is very large.
candidates.title: Attacker-controlled multipart boundary length is not bounded before use in MultipartStream (potential CPU/memory DoS)

counter_evidence: sizeMax and fileSizeMax exist and are documented as controls for total request size and single-file size (lines 157-167); an operator setting sizeMax strictly bounds the number of parts that can fit in a request, indirectly limiting the count.
The ProgressNotifier 'items' counter (lines 112 and 142-145) demonstrates that per-item counting already exists in the code base, though observed only for progress reporting.
No read source shows the parseRequest loop, so it cannot be shown that any part-count ceiling is actually absent from the execution path.
candidates.description: The read portion of FileUploadBase declares only sizeMax and fileSizeMax, both defaulting to -1 (lines 161 and 167), and documents these merely as the maximum complete-request size and per-file size. No field, constant, or accessor for a maximum number of parts/items was observed in the 1-200 line span, and RELEASE-NOTES.txt (version 1.3) likewise lists no such feature. MultipartStream itself keeps an item counter only for progress notification (items at line 112, incremented in noteItem() at lines 142-145) with no enforcement role. If parseRequest iterates parts without an independent count ceiling, a request containing a very large number of tiny parts could force per-part work (item creation, DiskFileItem temp handling, notifier callbacks) proportional to the part count rather than to payload size, a resource-consumption pattern. This conclusion is heavily qualified because parseRequest itself, where any such counting loop or guard would live, is outside the read spans.
missing_evidence: FileUploadBase.parseRequest (beyond line 200) was not read; it may contain a part-count or iteration limit not visible here.
FileUploadBase.getBoundary and getContentLength/deferred parsing logic that could bound iteration were not inspected.
No evidence of default or documented guidance on part-count limits, and no test or configuration reviewed to confirm the effective default behavior.
preconditions: Application invokes FileUploadBase.parseRequest on untrusted multipart input and does not supply its own part-count ceiling in the surrounding code.
The multipart body can legitimately contain a large number of small parts and is accepted by the container up to the request-size limit.
sizeMax is either -1 (the default) or set large enough to permit many small parts.
candidates.title: No per-request part count limit in the read portion of FileUploadBase (unbounded number of multipart parts)
